sorular.konu: LLM size and the memory problem (weights and KV cache)
sorular.soru: A large model fits on one GPU, but it still produces each new token slowly. What is the main reason?
secenekler: For each new token, the model processes the whole prompt again from the start
For each new token, the GPU turns all weights into a higher precision first
For each new token, the GPU must read every weight of the model from memory
For each new token, the model runs a small training step on all its weights
sorular.aciklama: To make one new token, the GPU must read every weight from memory, so a bigger model means more reading and slower tokens. The KV cache keeps the keys and values of old tokens, so the model does not process the whole prompt again.

sorular.konu: Quantization basics: number formats, scale, and rounding
sorular.soru: Which sentence best describes what quantization does to a model?
secenekler: It sets the least important weights to zero and keeps the others
It keeps every weight but stores each one with fewer bits
It trains a smaller model to copy the outputs of the big model
It replaces each weight matrix with two thinner matrices
sorular.aciklama: Quantization keeps all the weights and stores each number with fewer bits, which saves memory but adds a small rounding error. Setting the least important weights to zero is pruning, which removes weights instead of storing them more cheaply.

sorular.konu: Quantization basics: number formats, scale, and rounding
sorular.soru: Quantization stores small integers plus one scale for each group of weights. Why does it need the scale?
secenekler: It marks which weights were set to zero so the GPU can skip them
It saves the rounding error of each weight so it can be undone later
It shows which values are outliers that must stay in high precision
It turns the integers back into values close to the real weights
sorular.aciklama: Each integer counts steps on the grid, and the scale is the size of one step, so integer times scale gives a value close to the real weight. The rounding error is not saved anywhere, because saving it would cost as much memory as the weights.

sorular.konu: The outlier problem, granularity, and calibration
sorular.soru: Giving each small group of weights its own scale improves quality. Why don't methods give every single weight its own scale?
secenekler: The scales alone would then cost more memory than the fewer bits save
The rounding error would grow, because each scale covers fewer values
The grid would then have fewer steps, so each weight would lose precision
Per-weight scales only work with QAT, so the model would need retraining
sorular.aciklama: Every group stores one extra scale, so one scale per weight would cost more memory than the fewer bits save. Smaller groups lower the rounding error instead of raising it, because each scale fits its few values more closely.

sorular.konu: Weight / activation / KV-cache quantization and LLM.int8()
sorular.soru: Plain 8-bit quantization works well for smaller models but breaks down for very large ones. What changes as the models grow?
secenekler: All values grow larger together, so each value needs more bits to store
Most weights grow very small, so they round to zero much more often than before
A few hidden features grow huge, so one scale cannot fit them and the rest
The weights become more alike, so the grid can no longer tell them apart
sorular.aciklama: In large models a few hidden features become much larger than the rest, so one shared scale cannot fit both them and the normal values. If all values grew together, one bigger scale would still fit them all, so more bits would not be needed.

sorular.soru: PTQ works well for most models, but at very low bit widths it can lose too much quality. Why can QAT do better there?
secenekler: It uses a larger calibration set, so the range is chosen more exactly
It trains with rounding in the loop, so the weights adapt to the grid
It keeps the outliers in high precision, so no large errors remain
It drops the weights that round badly, so the rest stay more precise
sorular.aciklama: QAT puts the rounding into training, so the weights can adapt to a very coarse grid, but it costs a training run. A larger calibration set only helps PTQ place its range better, and it cannot teach the weights to handle the rounding.

sorular.soru: A team can prune freely, or use a fixed pattern that keeps two of every four weights. Why might it choose the fixed pattern?
secenekler: It keeps more quality than free pruning at the same sparsity
It turns the model into a smaller dense model with fewer layers
It fits GPU kernels that skip the zeros, so it can run faster
It needs no extra memory to store where the kept weights are
sorular.aciklama: The fixed pattern is regular, so many GPUs have kernels that skip its zeros and give real speed. The price is a little more quality loss than free pruning, because the pattern forces which weights can go.

sorular.konu: Pruning scoring methods: Magnitude, Wanda, SparseGPT
sorular.soru: A team prunes a medical chatbot. For the importance scores, it uses example texts from children's stories. What is the main risk?
secenekler: The scores may not match medical inputs, so useful weights get removed
The model may start to write stories, because pruning trains on the texts
The weights that stories use may be cut, so the model loses story skills
The zeros may fall in a random pattern, so the GPU cannot skip them
sorular.aciklama: The scores measure how much each weight matters on the example texts, so weights needed only for medical questions can look unimportant and get cut. Weights that stories use get high scores and stay, so the danger is to the medical skills.

sorular.konu: Pruning scoring methods: Magnitude, Wanda, SparseGPT
sorular.soru: When one pruning method removes a weight, it also changes some of the weights that are left. What is the goal of these changes?
secenekler: To make the remaining weights small enough to store in fewer bits
To move the zeros into a regular pattern that the GPU can skip
To retrain the layer on labeled data so that it relearns the task
To keep the layer's outputs almost the same as before the removal
sorular.aciklama: Deleting a weight moves the layer's output a little, and changing the weights that are left can cancel most of that change. This happens in one pass on example inputs, with no labels and no retraining, so it is not a fine-tuning step.

sorular.konu: Structured pruning, low-rank factorization, and recovery
sorular.soru: Pruning and low-rank factorization both make a weight matrix cheaper to store. How are they different?
secenekler: Pruning keeps the matrix in a smaller form, while low-rank removes parts of it
Pruning removes parts of the matrix, while low-rank keeps it in a smaller form
Pruning stores each weight in fewer bits, while low-rank sets small ones to zero
Pruning always needs a teacher model, while low-rank needs no training at all
sorular.aciklama: Pruning deletes some weights or whole rows, while low-rank factorization keeps the whole matrix and writes it as two thin matrices with fewer numbers. Low-rank does not delete parts of the matrix, and storing weights in fewer bits is quantization, not pruning.

sorular.konu: Knowledge distillation: soft targets and temperature
sorular.soru: A student model is weak on legal questions. It learned only from its teacher, and the teacher is weak there too. What would help most?
secenekler: Use a teacher that is strong on legal questions and filter its bad answers
Raise the temperature so the student sees more of the teacher's preferences
Make the student bigger so it can take in more from the same teacher
Train longer on the same teacher outputs so the student copies them better
sorular.aciklama: A student can only learn what its teacher shows it, so the real fix is a better teacher and cleaner teacher data. A bigger student or more training on the same outputs would only copy the same gaps more closely.

sorular.konu: Knowledge distillation: soft targets and temperature
sorular.soru: The teacher predicts the next word: 'cat' gets a high probability, 'dog' a small one, and 'car' almost zero. What does the student learn from this?
secenekler: That 'cat' is right and every other word is equally wrong
That 'dog' fits a little here, but 'car' does not fit at all
That the teacher is unsure, so this example should be thrown away
That 'dog' will become the top answer once the temperature is raised
sorular.aciklama: Soft targets keep the teacher's small probabilities, and these show which wrong answers are close to the right one. A hard label only says 'cat' and treats 'dog' and 'car' as equally wrong, so it carries much less information.

sorular.konu: Knowledge distillation: soft targets and temperature
sorular.soru: We soften the teacher's outputs with a higher temperature. What stays the same?
secenekler: The probability of the top answer
The gap between the top answer and the rest
The small probabilities of the other answers
The answer with the highest probability
sorular.aciklama: Temperature divides every logit by the same number, so the order of the answers does not change and the top answer stays on top. The probability of the top answer does change: it goes down while the small probabilities go up.

sorular.konu: KD loss and types of knowledge
sorular.soru: A team can reach a big teacher only through an online service that returns text. Which kind of distillation can it still do?
secenekler: Train the student to match the teacher's hidden states
Train the student to match the teacher's softened logits
Train the student to match the teacher's written answers
Train the student to match how the teacher's features relate
sorular.aciklama: A service that returns only text shows what the teacher writes, so the student can still learn from those answers. Logits, hidden states and feature relations live inside the teacher, so they need white-box access to its internals.

sorular.konu: KD case studies: DistilBERT/TinyBERT, Step-by-Step, Minitron
sorular.soru: In step-by-step distillation, the student learns to write the teacher's reasons, but at test time it gives only the answer. Why learn the reasons at all?
secenekler: Writing reasons is an extra task that shows the student how to get the answer
Writing reasons lets the teacher check each answer of the student at test time
Writing reasons replaces the answer labels, so no answer data is needed at all
Writing reasons makes the student bigger, so it can hold more of the knowledge
sorular.aciklama: Writing the reason is a second training task, and it gives the student a richer signal about how the answer is reached. At test time only the answer task runs, so there is no teacher and no reason, and the answer task still uses answer labels in training.

sorular.konu: KD case studies: DistilBERT/TinyBERT, Step-by-Step, Minitron
sorular.soru: A team needs a smaller model. Pruning its big model and then distilling from it needs far less training than starting from zero. Why?
secenekler: The small model keeps all weights in fewer bits, so it has nothing to relearn
The small model gets fresh random weights, so soft targets teach it faster
The small model uses soft targets only, so it needs no training text at all
The small model starts from trained weights, so it only has to recover
sorular.aciklama: Pruning keeps most of the trained weights, so the smaller model already knows a lot and distillation only has to repair what was lost. A student with fresh random weights would have to learn everything again, which is the costly path from zero.

sorular.konu: KV-cache compression and choosing a method
sorular.soru: To keep the KV cache small in a very long chat, one method keeps only the first and the most recent tokens. What is the risk?
secenekler: Each kept token is stored in fewer bits, so all its values lose precision
The model can no longer see the dropped tokens, so it may miss facts
Several query heads must share one key-value head, so quality drops
The model must run the prefill again for every token that it drops
sorular.aciklama: Evicting tokens frees memory by deleting their keys and values, so later tokens cannot attend to them and facts from the middle of the chat can be lost. Storing values in fewer bits is quantization, a different method that keeps every token.

sorular.konu: KV-cache compression and choosing a method
sorular.soru: A model's weights are too big for the team's GPU. Chats are short, and speed is fine. The team wants a cheap first step. What fits best?
secenekler: KV-cache compression, since it shrinks memory that grows with chat length
Structured pruning, since it gives real speed on normal hardware
Distillation, since it trains a new and smaller model from the big one
Quantization, since it stores each weight in fewer bits with no retraining
sorular.aciklama: When the weights are the problem, quantization is the usual first step, because it shrinks every weight and PTQ needs no training run. KV-cache compression helps with long chats and many users, but here the chats are short, so the cache is not the problem.
